Fixes an issue where users in a shared group or channel session could ask about an earlier message but the agent could no longer tell which participant sent that historical turn.

## Why This Change Was Made

Reuses the sender fields already persisted on ordinary session user turns. At the shared LLM boundary, the current runtime turn is correlated with its exact post-write transcript row and sender attribution is rendered through the existing untrusted conversation-context format. Agents can reliably answer who said what across turns in an existing group session. Current-turn sender handling, pre-activation channel history, DMs, and session routing remain unchanged.

target.title: fix(codex): guard sandbox http/request JSON.parse against non-JSON stdout
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`runSandboxHttpRequest` in `extensions/codex/src/app-server/sandbox-exec-server/http.ts` parsed the sandbox shell helper's stdout with an unguarded `JSON.parse`. When the helper exits 0 but emits non-JSON output, the raw `SyntaxError` can include the helper output and is returned through the exec-server JSON-RPC error boundary without identifying `sandbox http/request`.

## Why This Change Was Made

The Codex exec-server protocol requires buffered `http/request` responses to use the `{ status, headers, bodyBase64 }` envelope. This change guards that plugin-owned helper-envelope parse boundary and replaces raw parse diagnostics with one attributable, generic error. Valid envelopes and the upstream Codex protocol remain unchanged.

The shared sanitizing parser now covers buffered and streaming helper stdout. Focused WebSocket regressions verify the exact JSON-RPC message and prove a representative daemon banner is absent in both modes. The resulting JSON-RPC error is the standard internal error (`-32603`), not a custom error type.

## User Impact

A Codex `http/request` tool whose sandbox helper emits non-JSON stdout now fails with `sandbox http/request returned non-JSON stdout` instead of an opaque parse diagnostic. Raw helper output is not disclosed in that error. Valid JSON responses are unchanged.

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior addressed:** A successful sandbox helper process that emitted non-JSON stdout produced a raw parse diagnostic at the exec-server JSON-RPC boundary.
- **Real environment tested:** Linux x86_64, Node v26.5.0, commit `f39b109612d5156a86d990bba874951a1d1cf12c` on branch `fix/codex-sandbox-http-jsonparse-guard`, rebased onto `upstream/main` `a61f6b75ab74070161dc93db48a643c8a25146ee`.
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:** `node --import tsx /tmp/verify-codex-sandbox-http-real.mts` and `node --import tsx /tmp/verify-codex-sandbox-http-streaming-real.mts` start the real exported OpenClaw Codex exec-server, open real WebSockets, issue `initialize` and buffered/streaming `http/request` requests, and drive both real helper-output parse paths. Only the injected sandbox backend is controlled so it can deterministically return exit code 0 with `not-json <html>daemon warning</html>`; the server, WebSocket, JSON-RPC dispatch, response parsing, and error serialization are real.
- **Evidence after fix:** Terminal capture of `node` runtime verification (live stdout, copied verbatim):

  ```text
  $ node --import tsx /tmp/verify-codex-sandbox-http-real.mts
  rpcCode=-32603
  message="sandbox http/request returned non-JSON stdout"
  rawStdoutDisclosed=false
  result=PASS

  $ node --import tsx /tmp/verify-codex-sandbox-http-streaming-real.mts
  rpcCode=-32603
  message="sandbox http/request returned non-JSON stdout"
  rawStdoutDisclosed=false
  result=PASS
  node=v26.5.0
  ```

- **Observed result after fix:** Both buffered and streaming real WebSocket JSON-RPC paths return internal-error code `-32603` with exactly `sandbox http/request returned non-JSON stdout`; neither `daemon warning` nor the HTML helper output appears in either message.
- **What was not tested:** A production sandbox backend spontaneously emitting a banner. The deterministic backend injection is required to create that otherwise nondeterministic output, while the full exec-server/WebSocket/JSON-RPC/parse boundary is exercised. The valid-envelope regression is covered by the focused suite.

## Tests and validation

```text
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run extensions/codex/src/app-server/sandbox-exec-server.http.test.ts
Test Files  1 passed (1)
Tests       8 passed (8)

$ ./node_modules/.bin/oxfmt --check extensions/codex/src/app-server/sandbox-exec-server/http.ts extensions/codex/src/app-server/sandbox-exec-server.http.test.ts
All matched files use the correct format.

$ node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs --tsconfig config/tsconfig/oxlint.extensions.json extensions/codex/src/app-server/sandbox-exec-server/http.ts extensions/codex/src/app-server/sandbox-exec-server.http.test.ts
Found 0 warnings and 0 errors.

$ node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p tsconfig.extensions.json --incremental --tsBuildInfoFile /tmp/openclaw-98881-extensions.tsbuildinfo
(exit 0)

$ node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p test/tsconfig/tsconfig.extensions.test.json --incremental --tsBuildInfoFile /tmp/openclaw-98881-extension-tests.tsbuildinfo
(exit 0)

$ node scripts/build-all.mjs
(exit 0)
```

Dependency contract checked directly at OpenAI Codex source commit `7f3eb8a2233aceba3e7962123da84379ee305bb2`: `codex-rs/exec-server-protocol/src/protocol.rs` defines the `http/request` request and `{ status, headers, bodyBase64 }` response envelope; `codex-rs/exec-server/src/client/rpc_http_client.rs` sends it through the shared JSON-RPC client.

## Risk checklist

- User-visible behavior: Yes (intended and bounded): malformed successful helper output now has an attributable sanitized error.
- Config/env/migration behavior: No.
- Security/auth/secrets/network/tool execution: Security improvement only; raw helper stdout is not copied into the error and no execution path changes.
- Plugins/providers/channels/SDK: Codex plugin-internal implementation; no SDK or protocol shape changes.
- Highest-risk area: accidental differences between buffered and streaming malformed-output handling.
- Mitigation: buffered and streaming valid/malformed regressions, exact message/non-disclosure assertions, two real WebSocket JSON-RPC runtime proofs, LOC ratchet, prod/test type gates, lint/format, and full build.

The preceding exact-head CI failures were inspected from the job logs. target.title: fix(skills): globally-installed ClawHub skills falsely show as not tracked [AI-assisted]
target.body:
> [AI-assisted] This PR was generated using Claude Code.

Closes #105530

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users who install a ClawHub skill **globally** (`openclaw skills install <slug> --global`, living under the managed dir `~/.openclaw/skills/<slug>` and tracked in the **global** lockfile `~/.openclaw/.clawhub/lock.json`) would see the skill falsely reported as `ClawHub link invalid` in `openclaw skills status` and the Control UI, with the message:

> Skill `<slug>` has ClawHub origin metadata but is not tracked by the workspace ClawHub lockfile.

The skill is in fact correctly installed and tracked - just in the global lockfile, not the workspace one.

## Why This Change Was Made

`buildWorkspaceSkillStatus` read the ClawHub lockfile exclusively from the workspace directory (`readClawHubSkillsLockfileStatusSync(workspaceDir)`) and passed that single read to `resolveClawHubSkillStatusLinkSync` for every non-bundled skill. For a globally-installed skill (`source: "openclaw-managed"`), the tracking entry lives in the **managed** lockfile at `<dirname(managedSkillsDir)>/.clawhub/lock.json`, so the workspace lookup misses it and returns `invalid`.

The fix resolves the link status for `openclaw-managed` skills against the managed lockfile (and the managed parent dir, so the expected-install-dir check matches the skill dir) instead of the workspace lockfile. Workspace-local skills are unchanged. Detection uses the loader-assigned `source` rather than a lexical path check, because managed skill roots may contain symlinks whose resolved `baseDir` sits outside the `managedSkillsDir` tree.

## User Impact

Globally installed ClawHub skills now show as correctly `linked` in `openclaw skills status` and the Control UI skills view, instead of a false `ClawHub link invalid` / "not tracked" warning. Workspace-local skill status is unaffected.

## Evidence

Real behavior proof captured on Windows 10 by running the production `buildWorkspaceSkillStatus` against real on-disk lockfiles (standalone `tsx` repro script run locally; before/after output below). The script creates a managed (global) install - skill dir under `managedSkillsDir` with `.clawhub/origin.json`, plus a global lockfile at `<managedParent>/.clawhub/lock.json` tracking it - and a separate workspace whose own lockfile does **not** track the skill.

BEFORE (unpatched main) - the globally-installed skill is falsely `invalid`, read against the **workspace** lockfile:

```
"skillSource": "openclaw-managed",
"clawhub": {
  "status": "invalid",
  "valid": false,
  "reason": "Skill \"agentreceipt\" has ClawHub origin metadata but is not tracked by the workspace ClawHub lockfile.",
  "slug": "agentreceipt",
  "lockPath": "...\\openclaw-workspace-fYctHw\\.clawhub\\lock.json"
}
```

AFTER (this patch) - the same skill is correctly `linked`, read against the **managed (global)** lockfile:

```
"skillSource": "openclaw-managed",
"clawhub": {
  "status": "linked",
  "valid": true,
  "registry": "https://clawhub.ai",
  "slug": "agentreceipt",
  "installedVersion": "1.2.3",
  "lockPath": "...\\openclaw-managed-83CHpB\\.clawhub\\lock.json"
}
```

Regression tests added in `src/skills/discovery/status.test.ts`:
- links a globally-installed skill via the managed lockfile (asserts `status: "linked"`)
- reports a globally-installed skill as `invalid` when it is absent from the managed lockfile (guards against falsely linking)

Full skill-status suite passes (`pnpm test -- src/skills/discovery/status.test.ts` -> 13 passed, 1 skipped on win32).

## Real Behavior Proof

- Behavior addressed: Globally installed ClawHub skills (`source: "openclaw-managed"`) are falsely reported as `invalid` / "not tracked by the workspace ClawHub lockfile" because `buildWorkspaceSkillStatus` only consults the workspace lockfile.
- Real environment tested: Windows 10, Node v22.22.3, OpenClaw main @ 50e5ffcd25, running the production `buildWorkspaceSkillStatus` function from `src/skills/discovery/status.ts` via `pnpm exec tsx`.
- Exact steps or command run after this patch: a standalone `tsx` script builds a managed/global install (skill dir + `.clawhub/origin.json` + global lockfile tracking the slug) and a separate workspace whose lockfile omits the slug, then calls `buildWorkspaceSkillStatus(workspaceDir, { managedSkillsDir, entries })` and prints the resolved `clawhub` status.
- Evidence after fix:
```
AFTER (patched):
"clawhub": { "status": "linked", "valid": true, "slug": "agentreceipt",
  "lockPath": "...\\openclaw-managed-83CHpB\\.clawhub\\lock.json" }

BEFORE (unpatched main):
"clawhub": { "status": "invalid", "valid": false,
  "reason": "Skill \"agentreceipt\" has ClawHub origin metadata but is not tracked by the workspace ClawHub lockfile.",
  "lockPath": "...\\openclaw-workspace-fYctHw\\.clawhub\\lock.json" }
```
- Observed result after fix: The globally-installed skill resolves to `status: "linked"` against the managed (global) lockfile instead of `invalid` against the workspace lockfile. The `lockPath` in the resolved status now points at the global lockfile.
- What was not tested: End-to-end through a running gateway / live Control UI render; the real `openclaw skills status` CLI against a real `~/.openclaw` home. The proof exercises the real production status function with real on-disk lockfiles, which is the exact code path the CLI and UI consume.

## Human Verification

Verified: the production `buildWorkspaceSkillStatus` code path with real on-disk managed + workspace lockfiles (before/after), scoped `pnpm test` for the skills status suite, `pnpm tsgo` (type check), `pnpm format:check`, scoped `oxlint --type-aware` on the changed files. Not verified: Swift (skipped on Windows), full `pnpm test` suite, live Control UI rendering. Note: local `pnpm build` (tsdown) hit a V8 out-of-memory crash on this Windows machine (a known low-memory local-env quirk, unrelated to this 3-line logic change); relying on CI's build check on a properly-sized runner.

## Security Impact

- Does this change authentication, authorization, or trust boundaries? No.
- Does this change credential, secret, or token handling? No.
- Does this change sandboxing or process isolation? No.
- Does this change network boundaries or external API calls? No.
- Does this introduce a new trust boundary or change an existing one? No.

No CODEOWNERS secops paths are touched (`src/skills/` is not secops-owned). The change only affects which local lockfile is consulted for a status display.

## Compatibility / Migration

No config, API, CLI, or lockfile-format changes. The set of inputs/outputs of `buildWorkspaceSkillStatus` is unchanged; only the accuracy of the `clawhub` status for globally-installed skills improves. No migration required.

## Failure Recovery

If the managed lockfile read regresses, globally-installed skills would revert to the prior `invalid` / "not tracked" display behavior - a cosmetic status misreport, not a crash or data loss. The change is read-only with respect to lockfiles (no writes), so there is no risk of lockfile corruption. Reverting the commit fully restores prior behavior.

## Risks and Mitigations

- **Risk**: A skill whose loader-assigned `source` is `openclaw-managed` but whose lockfile entry legitimately lives in the workspace lockfile would now be looked up in the managed lockfile. **Mitigation**: managed skills are, by definition, installed under `managedSkillsDir` and tracked in the managed lockfile; workspace-local skills use other `source` values and are unaffected. Added a regression test for the "absent from managed lockfile" case to ensure such a skill still reports `invalid` rather than falsely `linked`.
- **Risk**: Competing/sibling PR on the same issue. **Mitigation**: this PR supplies the real-behavior-proof (real production-function output with real on-disk lockfiles, before/after) that the issue's proof gate requires, rather than a screenshot.

## Review Conversations

- [x] I will respond to review comments in the review conversation where they were left.
- [x] I understand review conversations belong to the reviewer and I should not resolve them myself unless requested.

target.title: fix: active-memory recall fails with billing rejections on subscription-only Claude CLI setups
target.body:
Closes #106839
Related: #86761

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where agents running on the Claude CLI runtime with subscription-only auth (Claude Code OAuth, no Anthropic API key) would have every active-memory recall either fail with a billing rejection (no extra-usage balance) or **silently draw paid metered extra usage** (extra usage enabled) — while main-session turns correctly ran on plan limits through the CLI backend. Anthropic routing direct anthropic-messages calls on subscription tokens to extra-usage billing is long-standing behavior; the embedded runner's direct-API passthrough (`cli_runtime_passthrough_openclaw`) was never a viable path for these credentials.

## Why This Change Was Made

Adds an opt-in `RunEmbeddedAgentParams.cliBackendDispatch: "subscription-auth"`: when the run's provider is `claude-cli` — directly or via a canonical `anthropic/<model>` ref whose configured `agentRuntime` is claude-cli — a backend is registered, and the ordered credential selection resolves to subscription (oauth/token) or nothing rather than an API key, the run executes through `runCliAgent` as a one-shot turn. Active-memory recall opts in. The dispatch preserves the embedded run's contracts:

- **Tool restriction is enforced server-side**: `toolsAllow` maps to the selectable-backend surface, bounds the loopback MCP grant (tools outside it can be neither listed nor called, even under bypass permission modes), and restricted runs get an exclusive loopback-only MCP bundle — user/plugin MCP servers are not merged in.
- **Transcript parity**: the run is mirrored into the caller-owned session file (user turn, live tool call/result records, assistant snapshot — flushed immediately on abort), so `persistTranscripts`, timeout partial-text salvage, and the live terminal-search watcher work identically to embedded runs.
- **Isolation**: fresh CLI process per run, no live-session reuse, session-scoped MCP cleanup (never the process-wide loopback server), CLI session bindings dropped from the result.
- **Scope**: claude-cli only; `google-gemini-cli` and custom backends keep the passthrough — their direct-API contracts were not verified and this PR makes no claims about them. An available API key keeps the existing fast passthrough. The core-side provider set could move to a `CliBackendConfig` capability flag if maintainers prefer that seam.

## User Impact

Subscription-only Claude CLI deployments get working active-memory recall on plan limits, consistent with their main turns — instead of failing every turn or silently consuming paid extra usage. Setups with an Anthropic API key see no behavior change. No config changes required; note that CLI-dispatched recalls measured 13.8–16.9s on a dev laptop, so the plugin's default 15s `timeoutMs` is tight — 30s is comfortable.

target.title: fix(agents): terminate mixed tool-call batches on critical loop veto
target.body:
Closes #106231

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users with loop detection enabled would keep burning model tokens for hours after a critical tool-loop action=block, because the blocked tool result was returned to the model normally and the agent loop continued indefinitely. The diagnostic log shows `action=block` repeating every 5-30 seconds for 2.8 hours after the first critical block until the user issued a manual `/stop`.

## Why This Change Was Made

The fix uses a **dual-layer termination strategy** to handle all batch shapes:

1. **Per-result** `terminate: true` — agent-core's `shouldTerminateToolBatch` stops the loop when every finalized result carries `terminate: true`. This handles single-tool batches and all-veto batches.
2. **Post-turn** `shouldStopAfterTurn` hook — scans `toolResults` for `deniedReason: "tool-loop"` after the batch completes. This covers mixed batches where the model emits the blocked loop tool alongside a normal tool call, because `shouldTerminateToolBatch` requires every result to terminate — a mixed batch never satisfies that condition.

Plugin-before-tool-call and plugin-approval vetoes remain non-terminating in both layers; only critical tool-loop vetoes trigger the stop.

This follows the canonical agent-core terminate contract (already used by client-hosted tools at `agent-tool-definition-adapter.ts:561`) rather than adding an independent abort path inside loop detection.

## User Impact

When loop detection reaches a critical threshold, OpenClaw blocks the looping tool **and** terminates the agent run so the model cannot keep retrying the blocked call — regardless of whether the model called the blocked tool alone or alongside other tools. Warning thresholds and post-compaction guard behavior are unchanged.

## Evidence

**Unit tests — terminate flag behavior (4/4 passed):**
```
agent-tools.before-tool-call.blocked-result.test.ts
  ✓ includes terminate: true for critical tool-loop vetoes
  ✓ does not include terminate for plugin-before-tool-call vetoes
  ✓ does not include terminate for plugin-approval vetoes
  ✓ defaults deniedReason to plugin-before-tool-call when omitted
```

**E2E tool-loop detection (83/83 passed):**
`expectToolLoopBlockedResult` asserts `record.terminate === true` on every critical block path (generic_repeat, known_poll_no_progress, ping_pong). All 83 tests green.

**Agent-core terminate contract (26/26 passed):**
Full `agent-loop.test.ts` suite green, including the critical proofs:
- "stops after a tool result only when the finalized result explicitly terminates" — proves per-result terminate for single-tool batches
- "stops after a mixed batch with one critical veto when shouldStopAfterTurn checks for tool-loop" — **new regression test** proving mixed-batch termination: two tools in one assistant response (veto + normal), post-turn hook catches the veto, loop exits after one turn
- "continues after a side-effect tool result when afterToolCall records it without terminate" — proves non-blocked results still continue

**Whitespace:** `git diff --check` — clean

**Format:** `oxfmt --check` on all touched files — clean

**Changes scope:**
```
 packages/agent-core/src/agent.ts                              |  7 ++++
 packages/agent-core/src/agent-loop.test.ts                    | 67 ++++++++++++++++++++++
 src/agents/agent-tools.before-tool-call.ts                    |  9 ++--
 src/agents/sessions/sdk.ts                                    | 14 ++++++
 4 files changed, 93 insertions(+), 4 deletions(-)
```

**Proof chain (how the fix works end-to-end):**

Layer 1 — per-result terminate (single-tool batches):
1. `buildBlockedToolResult({ deniedReason: "tool-loop" })` sets `terminate: true` on the blocked result
2. agent-core's `executeToolCalls` → `shouldTerminateToolBatch(finalizedCalls)` checks `every(finalized.result.terminate === true)` at `agent-loop.ts:807`
3. When every call terminates, the batch returns `terminate: true` → `hasMoreToolCalls = false` → loop exits

Layer 2 — post-turn stop (mixed batches):
1. After the batch completes, agent-core calls `shouldStopAfterTurn` with the final `toolResults`
2. `AgentSession.shouldStopAfterTurn` iterates `toolResults` looking for `details.deniedReason === "tool-loop"`
3. When found, returns `true` → loop emits `agent_end` before requesting another model turn

Both layers are independent: the per-result flag handles the common case, and the post-turn hook catches mixed batches. If either layer stops, the loop exits.

**Non-goals:** No changes to `loopDetection` config, warning thresholds, detectors, post-compaction guard, abort/signal machinery, or non-tool-loop blocked results.

target.title: feat: add Twilio RCS channel [AI]
target.body:
Related: #105710 (feature request / scope-fit discussion)
Related: #88476
Related: #102373
Related: #104862

## What Problem This Solves

OpenClaw can send and receive SMS through Twilio today, but SMS cannot carry most of the conversational surfaces OpenClaw is built around: no delivery/read receipts, no rich media or suggested actions, 160-character segment fragmentation, and an anonymous 10-digit sender identity. RCS restores those capabilities on a plain phone number, and core is already meeting real RCS traffic — #102373 (merged) had to teach the SMS channel to normalize Twilio `rcs:` addresses because Twilio Messaging Services with RCS senders are live in the field today. What is missing is a first-class channel: `rcs:+E164` targets, RCS webhooks, delivery/**read** status capture, **structured rich actions**, pairing/allowlist access control, and safe coexistence with existing SMS webhook setups.

## Why This Change Was Made

This adds an `rcs` channel plugin modeled on the existing SMS channel (#88476) while keeping RCS-specific behavior separate: RCS address normalization, outbound send handling, inbound webhook dispatch, status callback capture (including post-delivery `EventType=READ` read receipts), channel config metadata, plugin inventory/docs, and generated channel-config discovery are all included.

Beyond feature parity with the SMS channel's architecture, the channel carries the value that justifies it:

- **Read receipts and delivery states** — outbound status progresses through `sent`/`delivered`/`read` and is surfaced to the agent-visible status path (the same seam the SMS channel uses for delivery), so an agent can know a message was seen instead of guessing from silence.
- **Structured rich actions** — OpenClaw's portable `MessagePresentation` is translated into Twilio Content API create requests sent via `ContentSid` + `ContentVariables`: suggested replies, URL buttons, and rich cards are emitted through the RCS-supported `twilio/card` shape, while media-only messages use `twilio/media`. Inbound button taps arrive as `ButtonText`/`ButtonPayload` and are routed back as a normal agent turn. Content limits (1,600-character message/card bodies, suggestion title 20, postback id 200, up to 11 suggestions, card body vs 60-char subtitle) follow Twilio's documented Content API shapes; carousel and list-picker are documented as not-yet-emitted rather than advertised, and PHONE_NUMBER/dial actions (not expressible in the portable contract) are intentionally not built.
- **Verified sender identity** — an RCS sender is a carrier- and platform-vetted agent with a branded profile page (name, logo, description, contact details) instead of an anonymous number. For business and compliance-sensitive deployments this is a meaningful anti-spoofing/anti-phishing property, and the registration/vetting behind it is what compliance reviews typically ask for.

Provider posture mirrors the SMS channel: Twilio RCS Business Messaging is the initial supported provider, Twilio-specific webhook/API handling is isolated in the provider layer, and the channel surface itself (`rcs` id, `rcs:+E164` addressing, pairing policy, status capture) stays provider-neutral so additional RBM providers can back the same channel.

Hardening goes where the SMS channel has already been: the shared SMS/RCS Twilio webhook path now **fails startup loudly on an ownership collision** instead of silently going dark — the core plugin HTTP registry returns a `registered` flag (rather than an indistinguishable no-op unregister) that both the RCS and SMS channels consume, so a shared public route cannot leave a channel quietly disabled depending on startup order. The coarse rate limiter mirrors the SMS no-silent-drop behavior from #104862 by acknowledging signature-validated over-limit Twilio callbacks instead of returning a non-2xx that Twilio treats as delivery failure; the loopback SMS forward uses the SDK's guarded local-origin fetch rather than raw `fetch()`; outbound text passes through `sanitizeAssistantVisibleText`; and outbound CTA URLs are http(s)-guarded.

## User Impact

Users and operators can configure a Twilio RCS sender as an OpenClaw channel, send to RCS phone-number targets with suggested replies / buttons / cards, receive inbound RCS messages (including button taps routed back as agent turns), and collect RCS delivery/read receipts surfaced to the agent. Private deployments can use pairing or allowlists, while shared SMS/RCS Twilio webhook deployments now get a hard startup failure (not a silent no-op) on unsafe route ownership, plus documented setup constraints. Docs cover the RBM test-phase notice and launch expectations so operators are not surprised by client-side test banners.

This PR is AI-assisted.

## Evidence

Focused local validation on `upstream/main` base `23251474df0eb8ba27b70eba89a51c79e1e9d34e`:

- `git diff --check`
- `PNPM_CONFIG_VERIFY_DEPS_BEFORE_RUN=false OPENCLAW_VITEST_MAX_WORKERS=1 corepack pnpm test extensions/rcs extensions/sms/src/gateway.test.ts` — 12 files, **104 tests passed** (RCS rich-content request shapes, Content API create + send-by-ContentSid, inbound button-tap routing, shared-route collision in both startup orders, read/delivered receipt surfacing, plus SMS gateway regression coverage)
- `PNPM_CONFIG_VERIFY_DEPS_BEFORE_RUN=false OPENCLAW_VITEST_MAX_WORKERS=1 corepack pnpm test extensions/sms` — 11 files, **71 tests passed** (no regression from the shared `src/plugins/http-registry.ts` change consumed by SMS)
- Twilio Content API field names and limits cross-checked against Twilio's published Content API docs; the branch now emits RCS actions through `twilio/card` rather than standalone non-RCS quick-reply/call-to-action templates.
- `oxfmt --check` clean on changed files.

The heavier repo-wide lanes (full `tsgo:all`, full lint, import-cycle checks, shrinkwrap regeneration) are left to GitHub-hosted CI, which remains canonical for those gates. This branch is based on `23251474df` and can be rebased onto current `main` if bundled scope is sponsored.

On-device rendering of RCS rich cards/buttons and a captured live `EventType=READ` callback require a launched/approved RCS sender for the target carriers (an ecosystem prerequisite for any RCS implementation, not specific to this change); the outbound/inbound request construction and status handling are covered by focused unit tests, and provider signature/payload behavior is covered by Twilio signature/payload tests. Not live-tested against a production Twilio RCS sender in this PR branch.

target.title: fix(infra): accurate SQLite linkage wording for shared Node builds
target.body:
Fixes #106933

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users running OpenClaw on a Node build with shared system SQLite would see a startup/safety diagnostic claiming that Node **embeds** a SQLite version that actually came from the loaded shared library. That wording conflicts with `process.versions.sqlite` and steers remediation toward the wrong component.

## Why This Change Was Made

Keep the existing WAL-safety decision (loaded `sqlite_version()` remains authoritative). Only correct the diagnostic text: claim “embeds” when build metadata says Node is not shared-SQLite; say “shared SQLite … (loaded library; process.versions.sqlite may differ)” when `node_shared_sqlite` is true; use neutral “is using SQLite …” when the flag is unavailable.

Compatibility: diagnostic-only; no config/API/safety-floor change. Performance: reject path only. Usability: points operators at the real loaded library. Security: still rejects unsafe loaded versions.

## User Impact

On shared-SQLite Node builds, unsafe-SQLite errors now describe the loaded library accurately instead of saying Node embeds it. Embedded Node builds keep the previous “embeds” wording.

## Evidence

Verification host: local macOS (Crabbox bypass)

Commands:
- `pnpm exec oxfmt --check src/infra/node-sqlite.ts src/infra/node-sqlite.test.ts` → pass
- `node_modules/.bin/oxlint src/infra/node-sqlite.ts src/infra/node-sqlite.test.ts` → 0 warnings / 0 errors

Host metadata (this machine):
```text
node: 24.17.0
process.versions.sqlite: 3.53.2
process.config.variables.node_shared_sqlite: true
```

## Real behavior proof

- Behavior addressed: SQLite WAL-safety rejection diagnostics no longer claim Node embeds the loaded library when Node was built with shared SQLite.
- Environment: local macOS, OpenClaw checkout, Node v24.17.0 with `node_shared_sqlite=true` and `process.versions.sqlite=3.53.2`.
- Current-main contrast: `assertSqliteWalResetSafeVersion` always said `Node ${nodeVersion} embeds SQLite ${version}` even when the version came from a shared system library via `SELECT sqlite_version()`.
- Exact steps or command run after this patch:
  1. `node --import tsx -e 'import { describeLoadedSqliteRuntime, readNodeSharedSqliteFlag } from "./src/infra/node-sqlite.ts"; console.log(describeLoadedSqliteRuntime("3.46.1", process.versions.node, readNodeSharedSqliteFlag()));'`

  Node 24.17.0 is using shared SQLite 3.46.1 (loaded library; process.versions.sqlite may differ)

  Focused host-linkage test passed (1 passed / 20 skipped). Full suite: 21/21 passed.
- Control check: pure `describeLoadedSqliteRuntime` cases cover shared=`true`/`false`/`undefined`/`0`/`1`; safety still rejects unpatched loaded versions; “embeds” only when shared flag is false/0.
- Observed result after fix: shared host diagnostic names **shared SQLite** and the loaded version, and does not say “embeds SQLite”.

target.title: fix(shared): cap backtick delimiter length to prevent unbounded repeat
target.body:
## Summary
Cap `"` + "`" + `".repeat()` delimiter/fence length at 100 in `formatInlineCodeSpan` and `formatFencedCodeBlock` to prevent unbounded string allocation when content contains extremely long backtick runs.

## What Problem This Solves
In `src/shared/markdown-code.ts`, both `formatInlineCodeSpan` (line 23) and `formatFencedCodeBlock` (line 30) use `"` + "`" + `".repeat(longestBacktickRun(...))` without any upper bound. If the input contains a very long run of consecutive backticks, the generated delimiter/fence can be millions of characters long, causing excessive memory consumption or `RangeError`.

**Code evidence**:
- Line 23: `` const delimiter = "`".repeat(longestBacktickRun(value) + 1); ``
- Line 30: `` const fence = "`".repeat(Math.max(3, longestBacktickRun(text) + 1)); ``

Neither has a ceiling, so content with e.g. 100k consecutive backticks produces a 100k-character delimiter.

## Root Cause
`longestBacktickRun()` accurately counts backtick runs but its return value feeds directly into `String.prototype.repeat()` without validation. When the content itself is a large backtick run (malformed or generated input), the delimiter size mirrors the content size rather than being bounded.

## Why This Fix
Add `MAX_BACKTICK_DELIMITER = 100` constant and apply `Math.min(..., MAX_BACKTICK_DELIMITER)` to both call sites:
- `formatInlineCodeSpan`: `Math.min(longestBacktickRun(value) + 1, MAX_BACKTICK_DELIMITER)`
- `formatFencedCodeBlock`: `Math.min(Math.max(3, longestBacktickRun(text) + 1), MAX_BACKTICK_DELIMITER)`

A cap of 100 is well beyond any practical need (even content with 10+ consecutive backticks is rare) while being small enough to never cause memory issues.

## User Impact
- **Affected**: Any caller of `formatInlineCodeSpan` or `formatFencedCodeBlock` with content containing extremely long backtick runs
- **After fix**: Delimiter never exceeds 100 backticks, preventing memory issues

## Evidence
- **Before**: `formatInlineCodeSpan("` + "`" + `".repeat(100_000))` → delimiter length = 100001 (unbounded)
- **After**: `formatInlineCodeSpan("` + "`" + `".repeat(100_000))` → delimiter length = 100 (capped)

## Real Behavior Proof

### Before (on main)
```bash
$ node --import tsx proof.mjs
=== PROOF: Backtick delimiter cap ===

Test 1: formatInlineCodeSpan with 100,000 backtick content
  Delimiter length: 100001 (capped at 100)
  FAIL: Not capped

Test 2: formatFencedCodeBlock with 100,000 backtick content
  Fence length: 100001 (capped at 100)
  FAIL: Not capped

Test 3: Normal content unaffected
  PASS: Normal content works correctly
```

### After (with fix)
```bash
$ node --import tsx proof.mjs
=== PROOF: Backtick delimiter cap ===

Test 1: formatInlineCodeSpan with 100,000 backtick content
  Delimiter length: 100 (capped at 100)
  PASS: Capped — no crash

Test 2: formatFencedCodeBlock with 100,000 backtick content
  Fence length: 100 (capped at 100)
  PASS: Capped — no crash

Test 3: Normal content unaffected
  PASS: Normal content works correctly

=== All checks passed ===
```

## Tests and Validation
- `pnpm test -- src/shared/markdown-code.test.ts` — 12 tests passed (including 4 new regression tests)
- `git diff --check` — clean

target.title: fix(agents): repair interrupted tool calls at provider-bound replay seam
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Interrupted sessions (process crash, /new, or network drop during tool execution) leave orphaned tool_use blocks in persisted session history, causing Anthropic API to reject every subsequent resume with a persistent 400 error. Call the existing provider-aware `repairAttemptToolUseResultPairing` in the provider-bound replay path to synthesize error tool_results for missing pairs.

- Problem: OpenClaw sessions interrupted mid-tool-call persist orphaned tool_use blocks without matching tool_result. Anthropic requires each tool_use to be immediately followed by tool_result, so every subsequent run on that session fails with 400 — even across restarts. The existing `repairAssembledMessages` callback (in `tool-result-context-guard.ts`) only covers ongoing tool-result replay, not initial session resume.
- Solution: Gate `repairAttemptToolUseResultPairing` behind `transcriptPolicy.repairToolUseResultPairing` in `attempt.ts` at the two `buildSessionContext().messages → agent.state.messages` assignment points. This is the same provider-aware repair function and policy already used for tool-result replay, now also covering initial session resume.
- What changed: `src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/attempt.ts` (2 call sites wrapped with policy-gated repair, 0 net LOC growth).
- What did NOT change: `session-manager.ts` (untouched), `session-transcript-repair.ts` (untouched), non-provider consumers (compaction, transcript-file-state, etc.), the existing `repairAssembledMessages` callback path.

## Change Type

- [x] Bug fix
- [ ] Feature
- [ ] Refactor required for the fix
- [ ] Docs
- [ ] Security hardening
- [ ] Chore/infra

## Scope

- [x] Gateway / orchestration
- [ ] Skills / tool execution
- [ ] Auth / tokens
- [ ] Memory / storage
- [ ] Integrations
- [ ] API / contracts
- [ ] UI / DX
- [ ] CI/CD / infra

## Linked Issue/PR

- Fixes #106781
- Related to #106935 (concurrent PR by xydigitLybnnnn — targets session-manager.ts unconditionally)
- [x] This PR fixes a bug or regression

## Motivation

When a session is interrupted mid-tool-call (crash, /new, network drop), the session history in openclaw.sqlite retains a dangling `tool_use` block with no matching `tool_result`. On every subsequent run, Anthropic rejects the entire conversation history with a 400 error. OpenClaw retries 4 times then fails with "agent run failed before producing a reply."

The repair function chain (`sanitizeToolUseResultPairing` → `repairAttemptToolUseResultPairing`) was already integrated into the tool-result replay path via `repairAssembledMessages` in `attempt.ts:761`, but the initial session resume path (where this bug manifests) was missed. This PR adds the repair at that missing entry point using the same provider-aware function and policy gate.

## Evidence

- Behavior addressed: Orphaned tool_use blocks from interrupted sessions are repaired with synthetic error tool_results during initial provider-bound session resume.
- Real environment tested: Linux, Node 24.15.0, `repairAttemptToolUseResultPairing` applied to raw session context.
- Exact steps or command run after this patch:

```
npx tsx pr-proof.mjs
```

- Evidence after fix:

```console
$ npx tsx pr-proof.mjs

=== BEFORE repair (raw buildSessionContext) ===
  role=user
  role=assistant

=== AFTER repair (repairAttemptToolUseResultPairing) ===
  role=user
  role=assistant
  role=toolResult toolCallId=toolu_proof_001 isError=true
    text: "[openclaw] missing tool result in session history; inserted synthetic error result..."

=== VERIFICATION ===
  Orphaned tool_use present in raw: true
  tool_results in raw: 0
  tool_results after repair: 1
  Synthetic error result present: true
  Provider-safe (paired): true

✅ Proof complete: repairAttemptToolUseResultPairing fixes orphaned tool_use
```

Test matrix:

| Scenario | Before repair | After `repairAttemptToolUseResultPairing` |
|----------|--------------|----------------------------------------|

  - ✅ Cleanup symmetry: In-memory only, no SQLite/state side effects

The repair chain (`sanitizeToolUseResultPairing` → `repairAttemptToolUseResultPairing`) was introduced in PR #106151 and wired into `repairAssembledMessages` callback (`attempt.ts:761`), which only fires during tool-result replay (`tool-result-context-guard.ts:445`). target.title: fix(cron): skip deleteAfterRun and preserve counters for manual runs (#83538)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`openclaw cron run` (a manual/operator run) on a `deleteAfterRun` one-shot ("at") job used to delete the job on success — consuming the one-shot so its scheduled fire never happened (issue #83538). Manual runs also mutated `consecutiveErrors` / `consecutiveSkipped` counters and `nextRunAtMs`, corrupting the scheduled retry/backoff/next-run state that only real scheduler executions should own.

The root cause is that `applyJobResult()` had no notion of *who* triggered a run: manual, scheduled (timer), and the gateway on-exit watcher all shared one finalization path, so `shouldDelete` and the counter mutations fired for every successful run regardless of origin.

## Why This Change Was Made

Instead of inferring "manual vs scheduled" from run outcome (fragile) or a single boolean, this PR threads an explicit `CronRunOrigin` (`"timer" | "watcher-terminal" | "operator"`) from the run entry point through the whole finalization path. Origin is the accurate ownership model:

- `applyJobResult` derives `consumesOneShot` and `ownsSchedulerState` as `origin !== "operator"`, and records `lastRunWasManual = origin === "operator"`.
- Operator runs record the outcome only — they never consume a `deleteAfterRun` one-shot and never touch scheduler counters / `nextRunAtMs` / enabled state.
- `timer` and `watcher-terminal` runs keep consuming the run and owning scheduler state, preserving the merged on-exit `deleteAfterRun` contract from #104550 (a successful watcher-terminal one-shot is still deleted).

The invalid-persisted-run path (`skipInvalidPersistedManualRun` in `ops.ts`) previously hard-coded `origin: "operator"`. Because the gateway on-exit watcher reaches that path with `origin: "watcher-terminal"`, an invalid persisted watcher run was mis-attributed as operator, diverging scheduler-owned counters/alerts/terminal state from other watcher executions. The caller origin is now forwarded through preflight into that finalization so every path carries the true origin.

## User Impact

- Debugging/manually running a scheduled `deleteAfterRun` job no longer silently cancels its upcoming scheduled fire.
- Manual runs no longer corrupt retry backoff, auto-disable, or next-run timing of scheduled jobs.
- Gateway on-exit watcher-terminal one-shots continue to be consumed exactly as before (no behavior regression for the #104550 contract).
- Invalid persisted watcher-terminal runs are now classified with scheduler-owned semantics instead of operator semantics, keeping counters/alerts consistent.

## Evidence

Real-behavior proof at the current head, driving the **unmodified git-tracked source** — `applyJobResult()` in `src/cron/service/timer.ts` and the store mutation in `applyOutcomeToStoredJob()` — through all three origins on a `deleteAfterRun` one-shot. Run inside a `node:24-bookworm-slim` container (container node v24.18.0, the supported runtime floor is 24.15.0) with the repo's own vitest, and corroborated by the committed regression suite.

```
HEAD: 28b206ff7d61aa313005031177b79cb7416ae931
Loaded code:
  src/cron/service/timer.ts :: applyJobResult()
    consumesOneShot    = origin !== "operator"
    ownsSchedulerState = origin !== "operator"
    lastRunWasManual   = origin === "operator"
    shouldDelete       = wouldDelete && consumesOneShot
  src/cron/service/timer.ts :: applyOutcomeToStoredJob()
    if (shouldDelete) store.jobs = jobs.filter(e => e.id !== job.id)
  src/cron/service/ops.ts   :: skipInvalidPersistedManualRun()
    applyJobResult(..., { origin: params.origin })   // caller origin forwarded

PART A — OPERATOR PRESERVATION (deleteAfterRun one-shot, origin "operator", ok)
  shouldDelete=false  jobPresentInStore=true
  nextRunAtMs 1770372000000 -> 1770372000000 (unchanged)
  consecutiveErrors 0 -> 0   enabled=true   lastRunWasManual=true
  => one-shot NOT consumed, job preserved, scheduler state untouched      PASS

PART B — WATCHER-TERMINAL CONSUMPTION (same one-shot, origin "watcher-terminal", ok)
  shouldDelete=true   jobPresentInStore=false   lastRunWasManual=false
  => successful on-exit one-shot IS consumed/deleted (#104550 kept)       PASS

PART B2 — TIMER BASELINE (origin "timer", ok)
  shouldDelete=true   jobPresentInStore=false   => consumes/deletes identically  PASS

PART C — INVALID PERSISTED RUN, ORIGIN FORWARDING (status "skipped")
  watcher-terminal: lastRunWasManual=false  consecutiveSkipped 0 -> 1 (scheduler-owned)
  operator:         lastRunWasManual=true   consecutiveSkipped stays 0 (operator-attributed)
  => invalid runs now carry the true caller origin                       PASS

Harness result (container node v24.18.0, vitest 4.1.9): 4 passed (4)
Committed regression suite src/cron/service/ops.regression.test.ts: 21 passed (21)
OVERALL: PASS
```

The regression suite adds parametrized coverage asserting watcher-terminal invalid runs keep scheduled/consuming scheduler-state semantics while operator invalid runs stay operator-attributed.

target.title: feat(sessions): upstream liveness for adopted catalog sessions
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Closes #104804 (v1 scope per the recalibration comment).

The Session Catalog can browse and adopt external Claude Code / Codex sessions, but adopted sessions go silent afterwards: when the human keeps working in the upstream CLI/Desktop directly, OpenClaw records nothing, and coordinating agents keep acting on stale assumptions. The session-state awareness layer (#104636, #104815) had no producer for external activity.

## Why This Change Was Made

Adopted catalog sessions join the awareness layer; the existing notice/wake/`changesSince` machinery covers them with zero new notification code:

- **`adopted` signal-log kind** (log-only): `sessions.catalog.continue` records the session's external birth with catalog/host payload, idempotent per session.
- **Upstream-link registry** (`session_upstream_links`, shared state DB): composite `(session_key, agent_id)` identity (global-scope safe, mirroring `session_state_heads`); stores catalog/host/thread identity, the physical upstream ref, and a scan cursor. Written only at adoption — no write amplification on catalog lists. Same-source refresh preserves scan progress; any identity change (thread/host/kind or physical ref: Claude file path, Codex connection fingerprint) rebases the cursor.
- **Provider probing seam**: optional `checkUpstreamActivity` on `SessionCatalogProvider`; providers return activity descriptors, core records events (plugin boundary preserved). Claude probes stat-then-bounded-tail transcript JSONL with a forward scan cursor that never skips unclassified bytes; Codex probes app-server turn lists with an item-level `{turnId, userMessageCount}` marker so `turn/steer` appends are detected; adoption baselines include active turns while history import still stops at the last terminal turn.
- **Lifecycle monitor** (60s fixed cadence, named freshness-exception owner, started/stopped with gateway runtime): probes only adopted sessions with registered watchers; detected external human turns record `human_direct_message` on the adopted session key (burst count in payload) and flow through coalesced notices + immediate wakes + `session_status changesSince`.
- **Self-echo via positive provenance**: OpenClaw-authored upstream turns are recognized by exact outbound-prompt provenance (Codex mirror) and normalized own-transcript text matching (Claude); imported native history is tagged (`mirrorOrigin`) so it never masquerades as OpenClaw-authored. No time-window heuristics. Active runs defer scans without consuming markers.
- **Concurrency/clock hardening**: post-await CAS on link identity closes the record-from-stale-source TOCTOU; marker writes are CAS-guarded; upstream timestamps are clamped for event history and never drive bookkeeping clocks (a skewed upstream clock cannot age-out watch cursors); a corrupt session store skips one link, never the tick.

Consciously rejected (documented in code + docs): backfilling links for sessions adopted before this version — transient linkage with no shipped contract; re-continuing from the catalog opts in.

## User Impact

Adopt a Codex/Claude session from the catalog, have a manager watch it (`sessions_send watch:true`), then keep jamming in Codex Desktop or the Claude CLI: the manager now gets one coalesced stale-state notice and reconciles via `changesSince` before acting. No new config, no protocol changes, no UI changes.

## Evidence

- Built by Codex (gpt-5.6-sol, xhigh) against a frozen spec; seven adversarial structured-review rounds (gpt-5.6-sol, xhigh) surfaced and fixed 11 real defects across detection, provenance, concurrency, and clock domains — each with a regression test; final remaining finding consciously rejected with inline rationale.
- Test suites (all green): upstream links (13), monitor (11) incl. TOCTOU/clamp/isolation regressions, session-state events (21), gateway catalog methods (7), codex catalog (74) + upstream activity + marker baselines, anthropic catalog (17) + upstream activity (8) + import provenance.
- Codex app-server contract verified against sibling `../codex` sources (protocol/common.rs, v2/thread.rs, v2/thread_data.rs, v2/item.rs).
- `pnpm check:changed` green on Blacksmith Testbox (build-time run: LOC, SDK API/surface, typechecks, lint); rerun on final head + hosted CI on this PR.
- Docs: `docs/concepts/session-state.md` extended (adopted kind, upstream monitoring, limits incl. no-backfill contract); codex-supervision cross-link. SDK surface budgets bumped intentionally for the new seam exports.

target.title: fix(feishu): add chunk-idle timeout to inbound media download
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves
Fixes an issue where a stalled Feishu (Lark SDK) inbound media download body blocks the channel's agent-reply workflow indefinitely because the underlying Node.js `Readable` async iterator never settles on empty/stalled streams.

Additionally preserves the existing Feishu timeout policy: the per-chunk idle timeout is now threaded from the caller (`media.ts`) instead of being a hardcoded 30s value hidden inside the helper. Operators with configured timeouts above or below 30s get consistent behavior across connection and body-stall handling.

## Why This Change Was Made
- Wrap each `AsyncIterable.next()` call in `Promise.race` against a configurable timeout so stalled Lark SDK bodies cannot hang inbound dispatch.
- **Do NOT `await` iterator.return()** in the finally block — Node Readable async-iterator `return()` hangs when the underlying source is stalled (waits for a `readable` event that never fires), so awaiting it would block timeout error propagation.
- Export `FEISHU_INBOUND_MEDIA_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS` (30s), remove the hardcoded default from `saveMediaStreamWithIdleTimeout`, and make `chunkTimeoutMs` a required parameter. Callers (`media.ts`) thread the effective timeout through `saveFeishuResponseMedia`.
- No new config/env surface. The timeout constant matches Telegram `TELEGRAM_DOWNLOAD_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS = 30_000`.

Collision check: searched open PRs for `media-chunk-idle`, `FeishuInboundMediaTimeoutError`, `withChunkIdleTimeout`, `saveMediaStreamWithIdleTimeout`; no same-file or same-problem open PR was found.

## User Impact
**Before:** A stalled Feishu media download (e.g., dropped TCP connection after HTTP headers) hangs the agent's inbound processing forever. The hardcoded 30s idle cutoff also ignored operator-configured timeouts.

**After:** Stalled downloads time out after the configured per-chunk idle period (default 30s), the upstream Readable is cleaned up via `iterator.return()`, and the error propagates so downstream dispatch can proceed. Operators with custom timeouts get consistent behavior.

## Verification
- Exact head: `36b5b89de1c`
- `oxfmt --check` extensions/feishu/src/media-chunk-idle.ts media.ts media-chunk-idle.test.ts media-chunk-idle.proof.test.ts — All matched files use the correct format.
- `git diff --check` — passed; exit 0.
- Focused tests:

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/feishu/src/media-chunk-idle.test.ts -- --run --reporter=verbose
```

```
 Tests  9 passed (9)
```

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/feishu/src/media-chunk-idle.proof.test.ts -- --run --reporter=verbose
```

```
 Tests  3 passed (3)
```

- Mutation check (previously verified): temporarily restored `await iterator.return()` → test times out at 120s → removed `await` → test passes in ~50ms.

## Real behavior proof

Behavior addressed: stalled Node.js Readable (Lark SDK boundary) timed out via real `saveMediaStream`; progressing and multi-chunk Readables complete without timeout.
Real environment tested: Node.js 22.22.0, Linux x86_64, real `saveMediaStream` from `openclaw/plugin-sdk/media-store`, real Node.js `Readable` (same type Lark SDK `getReadableStream()` returns).

Proof output (real `saveMediaStream` path):

```
[feishu media idle production proof] boundary=Readable timed_out=true elapsed_ms=59 chunkTimeoutMs=50
[feishu media idle production proof] progressing_readable=true size=4 timed_out=false
[feishu media idle production proof] multi_chunk_readable=true chunks=3 total_bytes=1280 timed_out=false
```

Evidence:
- **Stalled Readable times out in ~50ms** (not 120s hang): `new Readable({ read() {} })` → `Promise.race([next(), timeout])` → rejects with `FeishuInboundMediaTimeoutError`.
- **Progressing Readable completes normally**: `Readable.from([jpeg])` → `result.size=4, contentType="image/jpeg"`.
- **Multi-chunk Readable**: 3 chunks totaling 1280 bytes, completes within deadline.
- **Custom timeout below 30s (5s)**: fake timers advance to 5000ms → timeout fires at exactly 5s.
- **Custom timeout above 30s (60s)**: fake timers advance to 60000ms → timeout fires at exactly 60s.
- **iterator.return() called exactly once on timeout**: spy confirms cleanup without hanging.
- **Negative control**: never-yielding `AsyncIterable` without idle wrap stays `still-pending` after 150ms.

What was not tested: installed Lark SDK transport with real Feishu tenant (requires Feishu developer account + public webhook). The tested `Readable` type is the exact same Node.js `stream.Readable` that Lark SDK's `getReadableStream()` returns; the idle timeout wrapper operates at the `AsyncIterable` boundary regardless of whether the Readable originates from the SDK or a test.

## Risk / Compatibility
Low. The `IteratorResult.return()` is fire-and-forget (`.catch(() => undefined)`) so stalled streams never block cleanup. The timeout constant (30s) is the same as Telegram's production idle floor. Timeout is now threaded from the caller so operators with configured Feishu HTTP timeouts can override it. No config, env, or API surface change. Existing media save paths (Buffer, ArrayBuffer, writeFile, Readable) all thread through the same wrapper.

Fixes an issue where slow Logbook background refreshes could stack a new status, days, and timeline request batch every poll interval, while an older day response could overwrite a newer user selection.

## Why This Change Was Made

Silent refreshes now use one state-owned in-flight slot, and load generations ensure only the current day request can publish results or loading/error state. Foreground loading behavior and gateway-day rollover remain unchanged.

## User Impact

The Logbook view no longer builds up repeated gateway work on slow connections, and switching days keeps the newly selected timeline instead of being replaced by a late older response.

## What Problem This Solves

Resolves a problem where WhatsApp maintained local copies of outbound media loading, audio transcoding, MIME classification, and base64 decoding even though canonical media owners already existed. The copies had drifted: injected media readers could silently widen local-file access, image optimization was not exposed through the SDK facade, and malformed base64 uploads could reach permissive decoding.

This moves WhatsApp onto the canonical media paths and deletes its local outbound loader. Existing transcode defaults remain unchanged.

WhatsApp-specific behavior stays local: MP3, M4A, and WebM voice inputs still transcode; Ogg/Opus remains the only direct voice-compatible form; document naming remains transport-specific; and the legacy retry helper is intentionally untouched.

## User Impact

Supported WhatsApp media sending and voice-note behavior remain the same. Injected media readers must now provide an explicit local-root boundary, malformed base64 and data URLs are rejected consistently, and oversized uploads are rejected from their encoded-size estimate before allocating the decoded buffer.

target.title: fix(config): warn when JSON5 comments are lost on config write
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

OpenClaw parses `openclaw.json` using JSON5, which supports comments. However, when the configuration is modified, the system saves back using standard `JSON.stringify()`, which strips all user-authored comments.

**Issue**: #105683

## Why This Change Was Made

The root cause is in `src/config/io.ts` where config writes use `JSON.stringify()` which cannot preserve JSON5 comments.

This PR implements a warning to notify users when their comments will be lost. The warning propagates through both human-facing channels (logger.warn / console.warn) and machine-readable result fields (`ConfigWriteResult.warning` / `ConfigReplaceResult.warning`), so callers using `skipOutputLogs` still receive the structured diagnostic.

## User Impact

### Before
- Users add comments to `openclaw.json` for documentation
- Any config modification silently strips all comments

### After
- Users receive a clear warning when writing config with JSON5 comments
- Warning appears on stderr (logger.warn / console.warn) in normal mode
- Callers using `skipOutputLogs` receive the diagnostic via structured `result.warning` field without stderr pollution
- The warning intelligently excludes false positives (URLs in strings)

## Evidence — Real Terminal Proof (Current Head `7ca9d62`)

### 1. Normal Mode — Human-Visible Warning

Real invocation of `createConfigIO(...).writeConfigFile(...)` without `skipOutputLogs`:

**STDERR:**
```
BEFORE (config with JSON5 comments):
```json5
{
  // Gateway: local development mode
  "gateway": { "mode": "local", "port": 18789 },
  /* Plugin section — entries go here */
  "plugins": { "entries": {} }
}
```

AFTER (written — comments stripped):
```json
{
  "gateway": { "mode": "local", "port": 18888 },
  "plugins": { "entries": {} },
  "meta": { "lastTouchedVersion": "2026.7.2", "lastTouchedAt": "..." }
}
```

STDERR (logger.warn):
  Config write will strip JSON5 comments from .../openclaw.json.
  Use a separate tool to re-add documentation comments after modifications.
```

**STDOUT (clean JSON, no warning contamination):**
```json
{"proof":"normal-mode","warningDelivered":true,"stderrWarningCount":1}
```

The warning fires on stderr before the destructive write. The written file is valid JSON with all comments removed. `result.warning` carries the diagnostic for structured consumers.

### 2. Quiet Mode — Machine-Readable (skipOutputLogs)

Real invocation with `{ skipOutputLogs: true }`:

**STDERR:**
```
CONFIG (with comments, skipOutputLogs=true):
```json5
{
  // quiet-mode config — comments stripped silently
  "gateway": { "mode": "local" }
}
```

STDERR after write (skipOutputLogs=true):
  (no output — quiet-output contract preserved)
```

**STDOUT (clean JSON, structured warning intact):**
```json
{"proof":"quiet-mode","warningDelivered":true,"stderrClean":true}
```

The quiet-output contract is preserved: stderr is completely clean, but the structured `result.warning` field still carries the diagnostic for machine-readable callers.

### 3. Include Config + False-Positive Tests

Unit tests cover the full surface:
- `io.write-config.test.ts`: warns on root comments, preserves quiet mode, no false positives (URLs, escaped strings, adversarial input)
- `mutate.test.ts`: warns on `$include` file comments, suppresses with `skipOutputLogs`

All tests pass (9/9 warning-related tests, CI green: fork run #29300262511).

### 4. Structured Warning Contract

The warning propagates through the public result surface:
- `ConfigWriteResult.warning?: string` — returned by `writeConfigFile()`
- `ConfigReplaceResult.warning?: string` — returned by `replaceConfigFile()`, inherited by `ConfigMutationResult<T>`

target.title: fix(gmail): preserve bind errors across watcher output chunks
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where the Gmail watcher enters an endless 5-second respawn loop when its gog serve process fails with an "address already in use" error under two independent conditions:

1. The error message is split across stderr pipe chunks (e.g. `"address alre"` + `"ady in use"`) and the per-chunk classifier misses the completed marker.
2. The final stderr fragment arrives after the child `exit` event but before `close`, so a restart decision made on `exit` never sees the completed marker.

A third edge case remains reachable even with chunk-carrying: when the combined stderr text exceeds the 512-byte retention window, `.slice(-512)` can discard a cross-boundary marker from the retained tail before classification runs.

## Why This Change Was Made

The stderr `data` handler now carries a bounded 512-byte tail across chunks and **classifies the untruncated combined text** before retaining only the last 512 bytes — so a marker completed across the old-tail/new-chunk boundary is detected even when the combined length exceeds the retention window. The restart decision moved from `exit` to `close`, so classification sees every fragment after stdio has drained before deciding whether to stop or to schedule a respawn. The close handler also detects spawn failures from Node’s undefined child PID and clears the failed watcher without scheduling a launch retry. Bounded to the optional Gmail watcher serve path; no config or public API change.

## User Impact

Operators with an already-running Gmail watcher (or a stale port binding) no longer experience an infinite 5-second respawn loop when starting a second watcher. The watcher correctly stops restarts and logs a clear diagnostic.

## Evidence

**Before (RED) — exit-before-final-stderr (real child_process):** With stderr delivery paused so Node's documented `exit`-before-remaining-stdio ordering appears, deciding restart policy on `exit` misses the bind marker and would respawn:

```
BEFORE (decide on exit): addressInUse=false, wouldRespawn=true
events: ["exit:1:addressInUse=false"]
```

**Premise:** Node emits `exit` before all stdio is necessarily drained; `close` fires after streams close. Node also guarantees `close` after a failed-spawn `error`, with `subprocess.pid` left `undefined`; the new guard distinguishes that launch failure from errors on an already-running child. `isAddressInUseError` matches `/address already in use|EADDRINUSE/i` against the untruncated combined stderr text so a cross-boundary marker is classified before the tail is truncated for bounded memory.

**After (GREEN) — same harness on `close`:**

```
AFTER (decide on close): addressInUse=true, wouldRespawn=false
events: [
  "exit:1:addressInUse=false",
  "data:\"listen EADDRINUSE: address alre\"",
  "data:\"ady in use 127.0.0.1:18788\\n\"",
  "close:1:addressInUse=true"
]
VERDICT: RED→GREEN
```

**After (GREEN) — real occupied-port production path:** Port `127.0.0.1:18788` held by a real `net.Server`; PATH fake `gog` that for `watch serve` calls `server.listen` and surfaces the OS error. Production `startGmailWatcher` → `spawnGogServe` ran once and stopped restarts (no second serve after 6.5 s):

```
[gmail-watcher] [gog] listen EADDRINUSE: address already in use 127.0.0.1:18788
[gmail-watcher] gog serve failed to bind (address already in use); stopping restarts. ...
SERVE_INVOCATIONS 1
```

**Negative controls:**
- A failed spawn emitting `error` then `close` does not schedule a respawn.
- Non-bind stderr split across chunks still schedules exactly one respawn.
- Complete bind marker still stops restarts.
- Exit-before-final-bind-fragment then `close` stops restarts (no respawn after 6 s).
- Cross-boundary marker with second chunk large enough to push combined beyond 512 bytes (824 bytes total):
  - Chunk 1: `"address alre"` → Chunk 2: `"ady in use "` + 800 bytes noise
  - truncate-before-classify would miss the marker; classify-before-truncate detects it → stops restarts.

**Focused tests:** After rebasing onto `upstream/main` at `6a5736ba`, Linux Node CI ran `src/hooks/gmail-watcher.test.ts` — 14 passed in 118 ms, including failed-spawn `error` → `close`, split-chunk, exit-before-final-stderr, exceeds-retention-window, and non-bind controls. Exact-head CI run 29301471326 passed all Gmail and relevant checks; its only failure was unrelated latest-main deadcode export `src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/attempt-session-boundary.ts:27` (`CurrentUserTimestampOverride`), outside this PR’s two-file diff.

**Diff stats:** source net +23 LOC, tests net +187 LOC; total +217/-7 across 2 files. `git diff --check` clean.

**Unverified:** Live upstream `gog` binary / Gmail API watch-start credentials on this host (fake `gog` on PATH exercised the real spawn + OS EADDRINUSE path instead).

target.title: fix: render assistant transcript headers safely
target.body:
Related: #99253

## What Problem This Solves

Assistant-authored Markdown can visually resemble a fresh transcript turn when it begins with shapes such as `user[...]`, `[timestamp] user:`, or `<User ...>`. That can blur the authorship boundary in chat surfaces even though the text is still part of the assistant reply.

This PR makes those supported shapes visibly inert at render/delivery boundaries. It does not change stored transcript/history bytes or introduce the broader fail-closed tool-execution policy tracked by #99253, which remains open.

## Why This Change Was Made

The earlier implementation rewrote Markdown text with custom delimiter scanning. The final implementation instead reuses the repository's existing Markdown-It pipeline in `packages/markdown-core`:

- a core rule runs after Markdown inline parsing and emits semantic assistant-transcript-role annotations;
- inline, fenced, indented, and image-alt code are excluded structurally rather than with regular expressions;
- spoilers, entities, emphasis, links, image alt text, blockquotes, headings, tables, chunks, and slices share the same parsed representation;
- active links and overlapping inline formatting are suppressed only for the marked role header;
- Control UI, Telegram, Slack, and Signal render rich inert markers; LINE and SMS add a plain assistant-authored-transcript label;
- final plain-text, Slack mrkdwn, Telegram HTML, rich-media, and chunk projections are checked after their transport-specific transforms, then reparsed through the same Markdown IR detector;
- header grammar, Markdown-It token annotation, IR projection, Control UI rendering/options, and generated Telegram HTML handling live in focused owner modules rather than oversized renderer files;
- oversized/error Control UI fallback uses one localized `Assistant:` marker and preserves escaped source text without reparsing it;
- message-end diagnostics use the same parser options and log safe metadata only, never assistant text.

No dependency, config, environment-variable, migration, or protocol surface was added.

## User Impact

Role-looking text remains readable and remains part of the assistant reply, but the supported header itself is rendered as an inert authorship marker. Ordinary prose and Markdown code examples keep their existing behavior. User-authored messages are never annotated by this assistant-only path.

Release-note context is captured here because root `CHANGELOG.md` is release-owned. The maintainer rewrite preserves @snowzlmbot's contributor credit with a `Co-authored-by` trailer.

## Evidence

PR head: `c1934bb11147f7690b15d3aba6001eb204946441`

Implementation commits: `8c15dc360bb6eedce6c4ecc36435219f31eccee2`, `9ec8c60d8e6`, `daa6b83d15769656de71d5532b8265ffb6b2708d`, `23b8f86580a`, `6f7990f421d`, `c1934bb1114`

- 317 focused parser/IR, Control UI, agent, TTS, LINE, SMS, Telegram, Signal, and Slack tests passed across eight shards.
- The adjacent Control UI message-rendering suite passed 89/89 after CI exposed and we fixed three stale option expectations.
- Regression coverage includes transport-native Slack links/date tokens, Telegram promoted HTML/rich-media captions, code exclusions, and final chunk-size accounting.
- `pnpm tsgo:all` passed across the full TypeScript project graph.
- Plugin SDK API baseline and public surface checks passed against current `main`.
- Targeted formatting and lint checks passed; `git diff --check` passed.
- The TypeScript LOC ratchet passed on committed head: all oversized legacy files are below their base size and every new module is below 500 lines.
- Dead-code export analysis confirmed the refactor's moved helpers are private rather than accidental public surface.
- Fresh autoreview findings for Telegram media captions and Slack date tokens were accepted, fixed, and re-reviewed. The final pass had no accepted/actionable findings after source-verifying two false positives against current `main` and Telegram's item-count limits.
- A new post-refactor autoreview passed with no findings and 0.96 confidence.

Real behavior proof:

- A real Gateway + qa-channel + fresh Chromium Control UI run kept assistant role markers distinct, preserved inline/fenced code, left user-authored text unmarked, exercised Gateway display projection, and proved an image-alt caption remains outside its role marker.
- On the final refactored tree, a real Gateway + mock provider + Telegram plugin/Crabline run passed the `telegram-assistant-transcript-role-boundary` contract 1/1, covering both an ordinary role-looking reply and promoted rich HTML.

## Risk and Rollback

This is display/message-delivery hardening across several renderers, so the main risk is formatting regression. Parser semantics, channel projections, chunk/slice preservation, oversized fallback, and live UI/Telegram delivery have direct coverage. Rollback is a normal revert; there is no data or config migration.

## Docs

No user-facing docs change. This is an internal rendering and diagnostic hardening change.
